issues.legal_issue: A res judicata bar cannot be applied when the plea was not properly raised and proved, and the prior adjudication concerned only part of the property in the later suit.
material_facts: The defendant did not plead res judicata in the written statement or raise it in the trial court or first appellate court.
The plaintiff introduced the judgment and decree in an earlier suit as evidence supporting the title of a predecessor-in-title; the defendant did not then raise res judicata.
The earlier suit concerned a 240-square-foot portion of the property, whereas the later suit concerned the entire property.
The High Court inferred the scope and effect of the earlier adjudication without the necessary pleadings and issues from that suit.
issues.conclusion: The plea of res judicata had neither been properly raised nor proved, and the later suit was not barred on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata is an estoppel by judgment founded on public policy, not a limit on the court’s jurisdiction. Its factual foundation must ordinarily be pleaded, an issue framed, and the prior pleadings, issues and judgment produced so that the court can determine what was in issue and decided; the plea cannot ordinarily be raised for the first time on appeal. A judgment containing sufficient detail may sometimes establish the necessary matters. In State of Punjab v. Bua Das Kaushal, the Court permitted an unpleaded plea where the necessary facts had been considered and the opposing party had an opportunity to rebut it. The plea may also be waived by failure to raise it appropriately. The Court relied on (Raja) Jagadish Chandra Deo Dhabal Deb v. Gour Hari Mahato, Medapati Surayya v. Tondapu Bala Gangadhara Ramakrishna Reddi, Katragadda China Anjaneyulu v. Kattragadda China Ramayya, Syed Mohd. Salie Labbai v. Mohd. Hanifa, Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal, Kali Krishna Tagore v. Secretary of State for India in Council, Pritam Kaur v. State of Pepsu, Rajani Kumar Mitra v. Ajmaddin Bhuiya, and Sha Shivraj Gopalji v. Edappakath Ayissa Bi.

rule.if: appeal_in_civil_property_title_suit and res_judicata_not_pleaded_below and prior_case_materials_insufficient and prior_case_concerned_only_part_of_property

predicates.appeal_in_civil_property_title_suit: The matter is an appeal in a civil suit seeking a determination of title to property.
predicates.res_judicata_not_pleaded_below: The party relying on the earlier judgment did not plead res judicata or raise it in the trial court or first appeal.
predicates.prior_case_materials_insufficient: The materials from the earlier case do not establish the pleadings, issues and matters actually decided there.
predicates.prior_case_concerned_only_part_of_proper: The earlier case concerned only a portion of the property later put in suit.

issues.definition: When a civil property-title appeal involves an unpleaded res judicata defence, insufficient materials about the earlier case, and an earlier case concerning only part of the property, the later suit is not barred by res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: A plea of adverse possession fails when the claimant previously asserted a right as a co-owner and does not plead and prove when possession became hostile to the owner.
material_facts: The defendant pleaded continuous, open and uninterrupted possession for longer than the prescriptive period and claimed to have perfected title by adverse possession.
In an earlier suit, the defendant claimed to be an adopted son and sought a share in the property, asserting a claim as a co-owner in possession.
The defendant did not plead how or when his possession became hostile to the title of the owners and did not substantiate the adverse-possession plea.
issues.conclusion: The adverse-possession plea was vague, unsubstantiated and without merit.
issues.legal_principle: A party claiming title by adverse possession must plead and prove how and at what point the possession became hostile to the owner. A prior claim of possession as a co-owner makes it necessary to establish when and how that claim changed into hostile possession. The Court applied the requirements of pleading and proof for adverse possession; it cited no earlier case in deciding this issue.

predicates.appeal_in_civil_property_title_suit: The matter is an appeal in a civil suit seeking a determination of title to property.
predicates.claimant_previously_asserted_coownership: The person claiming adverse possession previously asserted a right to possess the property as a co-owner.
predicates.hostile_possession_start_not_pleaded_or_: The person claiming adverse possession did not plead and prove when and how possession became hostile to the owner.

issues.definition: In a civil property-title appeal, a claimant who previously asserted co-ownership but did not plead and prove when possession became hostile cannot succeed on adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who establishes title to property may obtain possession of the portion not already covered by a decree in the claimant’s chain of title, while the portion already covered must be recovered by enforcing that decree.
material_facts: The plaintiff acquired the property through a chain of conveyances, and the trial court and first appellate court found title in the plaintiff’s favour.
A predecessor-in-title had obtained a decree declaring title to and awarding possession of a 240-square-foot portion of the upper floor.
The earlier decree concerned only that portion, leaving the remainder of the property for determination in the present suit.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to possession under the earlier decree for the portion it covered and to a decree in the present suit for the remaining property; the High Court’s contrary decision was set aside and the lower courts’ decrees were restored in part.
issues.legal_principle: The existing decree for the specified portion should be enforced through execution, while the plaintiff’s entitlement to the remaining property could be determined in the present suit on the evidence of title. The Court relied on no cited earlier case or specific statutory provision for this allocation of the means of recovery.

predicates.appeal_in_civil_property_title_suit: The matter is an appeal in a civil suit seeking a determination of title to property.
predicates.title_established_in_current_suit: The claimant’s title to the property is established on the evidence in the current suit.
predicates.earlier_decree_covers_only_part_of_prope: An existing decree in the claimant’s chain of title awards recovery of only a portion of the property later put in suit.

issues.definition: Where title is established in a civil property-title suit and an earlier decree covers only part of the property, the covered part is recovered by enforcing that decree and possession of the remainder is awarded in the current suit.

issues.legal_issue: A successful claimant in a suit for title and recovery of possession may obtain an inquiry into mesne profits for the period specified by the governing procedural provision.
material_facts: The plaintiff succeeded in establishing title and obtaining a decree for possession of property occupied by the defendant.
The plaintiff sought mesne profits in connection with the recovery-of-possession suit.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to an inquiry into mesne profits under Order XX Rule 12(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure, for the period between the suit and delivery of possession pursuant to the decree.
issues.legal_principle: Order XX Rule 12(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a decree for an inquiry into mesne profits in a suit for recovery of possession. The Court relied on that provision and cited no earlier case on this issue.

predicates.appeal_in_possession_suit: The matter is an appeal arising from a suit seeking recovery of possession.
predicates.claimant_succeeds_in_title_and_possessio: The claimant establishes title and obtains a decree for possession.
predicates.defendant_occupied_property: The defendant occupied the property for which possession is decreed.

issues.definition: When a claimant succeeds in title and possession in a possession suit against an occupying defendant, the claimant is entitled to an inquiry into mesne profits.
